The doctor was an old man, and when I woke him he looked very kind and pleasant. I told him my brother and I had been hunting on Spanish Island yesterday afternoon and had camped on part of a raft we found. Around midnight, my brother must have kicked his gun while dreaming, because it fired and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go over and treat him without telling anyone. We planned to come home that evening and surprise the family.

“Who’s your family?” he asked.

“The Phelpses, down there.”

“Oh,” he said. After a moment he asked,

“How did you say he got shot?”

“He was having a dream,” I said, “and it shot him.”

“An unusual dream,” he said.

He lit his lantern, picked up his saddlebags, and we set off. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like it. He said it was big enough for one person but didn’t look safe for two. I told him,

“Don’t worry, sir. It carried all three of us easily enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns. That’s what I meant.”

“Oh,” he said.

But he put a foot on the canoe’s edge and rocked it, then shook his head. He thought he’d look for a bigger boat. All the others were locked and chained, though, so he took my canoe. He told me to wait for his return or keep looking for another boat. Or, if I wanted, perhaps I should go home and prepare the family for the surprise. I said I didn’t want to. Instead, I explained exactly how to find the raft, and he left.

Before long a thought struck me. Suppose he couldn’t fix that leg in a moment, as the saying goes? Suppose it took three or four days? What would we do—lie around until he gave away the secret? No, sir. I knew what I’d do. I’d wait here, and if he came back saying he needed to visit again, I’d get to the raft myself, even if I had to swim. Then we’d tie him up, keep him with us, and head downriver. When Tom no longer needed him, we’d pay him what he deserved, or everything we had, and let him go ashore.

So I crawled into a pile of lumber to sleep. The next time I woke, the sun was high overhead! I shot out and hurried to the doctor’s house, but they said he’d left sometime during the night and hadn’t returned.

‘Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean Sir Simon—are you hungry? There’s a sandwich in my case. Would you care for it?’

‘No, thank you; I eat nothing these days. Still, it is most kind of you, and you are far nicer than the rest of your dreadful, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.’

‘Stop!’ exclaimed Virginia, stamping her foot. ‘You are the rude and dreadful and vulgar one; and as for dishonesty, you know perfectly well you stole paints from my box to touch up that absurd blood-stain in the library. First you used all my reds, even the vermilion, so I could paint no more sunsets. Then you took the emerald-green and chrome-yellow, until at last I had only indigo and Chinese white remaining, and could paint nothing but moonlight scenes, which are always gloomy to look at and by no means easy to do. I never gave you away, although I was extremely annoyed; and the entire business was perfectly ridiculous, for whoever heard of blood that was emerald-green?’

‘Well, really,’ replied the Ghost, somewhat meekly, ‘what else could I do? Real blood is very hard to obtain nowadays, and since your brother started the whole affair with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason at all why I should not use your paints. Colour, after all, is a question of taste. The Cantervilles, for example, have blue blood—the bluest in all England. But I know such things mean nothing to you Americans.’

‘You know nothing whatever about it. Your best course would be to emigrate and broaden your mind. My father would be delighted to provide your passage free; and although spirits of every description carry a heavy duty, you will have no trouble at the Custom House, since all the officers are Democrats. You would certainly be a great success in New York. I know any number of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars for a grandfather, and far more for a family Ghost.’

‘I doubt I should enjoy America.’

‘Because we have no ruins or curiosities, I suppose,’ Virginia remarked sarcastically.

‘No ruins! No curiosities!’ the Ghost replied. ‘You have your navy, and your manners.’

‘Good evening. I shall ask papa to give the twins another week’s holiday.’

‘Pray don’t leave, Miss Virginia,’ he cried. ‘I am so unhappy and lonely, and truly do not know what to do. I wish to sleep, but cannot.’

‘How absurd! All you need do is get into bed and blow the candle out.’

They constituted her life, dearer than any place hallowed by love, dearer than everything else upon the earth. The boys greeted the news of our departure with childish delight; Clara inquired whether we were bound for Athens. “Perhaps,” I answered, and pleasure illuminated her face. There she would see her parents’ tomb and the land rich in memories of her father’s glory. Silently and ceaselessly she had dwelt upon those scenes. Remembering them had transformed her childhood gaiety into gravity and filled her with lofty, restless thoughts.

Many beloved companions must accompany us, however humble they might be. There was the spirited yet obedient horse Lord Raymond had presented to his daughter; there were Alfred’s dog and a tame eagle whose vision age had clouded. Yet we could not draw up this list of favourites without grieving for our great losses and sighing deeply over all that must remain. Idris’s eyes filled with tears as Alfred and Evelyn brought first a treasured rose tree, then an exquisitely carved marble vase, declaring that each must come. They lamented our inability to carry away the castle and forest, the deer and birds, and every familiar, cherished thing. “Dear, foolish children,” I said, “we have already lost for ever treasures infinitely more valuable than these, and we abandon these things to save treasures beside which they count as nothing. Let us never forget our purpose and our hope; they will raise an unassailable barrier against this flood of sorrow over trifles.”

The children were readily diverted and went back to anticipating their future pleasures. Idris was gone. She had withdrawn to conceal her weakness; leaving the castle, she had descended into the little park and sought a lonely place where she could surrender to her tears. I discovered her embracing an ancient oak, her rosy lips pressed against its rugged trunk, while tears streamed freely and sobs and broken cries escaped her control. With overwhelming grief I saw the beloved of my heart so entirely overcome by sorrow! I drew her to me; feeling my kisses upon her eyelids and my arms enclosing her, she awoke again to the knowledge of what she still possessed. “You are so kind not to rebuke me,” she said. “I weep, and a sharp pang of unbearable grief rends my heart. Yet I am happy: mothers mourn their children, wives are bereaved of husbands, while you and my children remain to me.”
